summary:
Kabardino-Balkaria stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition is prohibited outright. The law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 bans gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and removes the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. Reporting published in June 2024 profiles transgender Russians caught between leaving and staying, and analysis from August 2024 describes a court-driven purge and mass emigration of LGBT Russians; for many transgender people emigration has become the only remaining means of living openly.

Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. The 2013 law targeted material concerning minors, and was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups, reaching content that promotes "non-traditional" sexual relationships, makes minors interested in gender transition, or gives minors a "desire to change their sex"; the provisions reach speech that justifies gender transition. Enforcement has grown sharply: more than 180 cases were brought under these provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines, while fines brought over 60 million rubles (about $765,300) into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025.

Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, charges have been brought for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in that movement or display of its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, drawn from both the administrative and criminal codes. Between March and May 2026, nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist. Within 48 hours of the 2023 ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ life through 2025, and in December 2024 a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented. In summer 2021 a transgender woman was lured by relatives to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, escaping only after police responded to a phone she had found.

Russia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, and does not treat gender-identity or sexual-orientation motivation as an aggravating factor in sentencing. The state does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community.

Entry and onward-protection context carries explicit warnings for LGBT travellers. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and includes language relevant to LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention. A 2024 law additionally bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions.

The North Caucasus, including Kabardino-Balkaria, is markedly worse than the national baseline. David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by the Human Rights House Foundation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the region and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families; working in exile, he attests to annual deterioration.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) treats the North Caucasus, including this republic, as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory finding on Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the region are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note documents systematic regional campaigns from 2017 to 2024, and states that the 2023 "extremist" designation exposes LGBT+ activity to 2 to 6 years' imprisonment, rising to 6 to 10 years for organising, with violence spreading beyond the region.
tangentialFactors:
The North Caucasus departs from the assessment the same UK Home Office note applies to Russia as a whole, which otherwise finds no general persecution on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. That exception is what makes Kabardino-Balkaria materially more dangerous for a trans visitor than the national figures alone suggest.

The regional pattern documented from 2017 to 2024 includes forced return to families, an outcome that intersects with the national ban on legal recognition: a trans person cannot obtain documents matching their presentation, which makes concealment and safe movement harder. Violence in the region is described as spreading beyond it, so an assessment built only on Moscow or St Petersburg conditions underestimates exposure.

The scale of the national enforcement regime gives context to local encounters with police. Fines of over 60 million rubles in the two years to mid-2025 and more than 180 propaganda cases in 2023 indicate an active prosecutorial habit rather than dormant statutes, and the 101 extremism convictions recorded to 30 June 2025 show that administrative and criminal routes are both used.

Comparison with Chechnya, which the UK note names alongside the region's other republics, is common in reporting on the North Caucasus. Isteev's wider regional framing suggests conditions in Kabardino-Balkaria are not isolated from neighbouring republics, and both US and UK government advisories warn about the whole of Russia rather than the region alone.

There is no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, no hate-crime designation, and no aggravating factor in sentencing for gender-identity or sexual-orientation motivation. Hate crimes against the LGBTQ community are not officially recorded by the state, so the absence of official data reflects recording practice rather than an absence of incidents.

Display of the rainbow flag or its colours has drawn extremism charges since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation, and organising LGBT+ activity is exposed to 6 to 10 years' imprisonment, with 2 to 6 years for participation, per the UK Home Office note of June 2025.

Coercive conversion is a documented risk: a transgender woman was held for nine months near Novosibirsk in 2021, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour.

The 2024 law barring adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries permitting gender transitions applies to residents as well as visitors, and no anti-discrimination remedy exists at republic level.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Kabardino-Balkaria has its own republic-level administrative or criminal provisions targeting LGBT expression, in addition to the national statutes, is not resolved by the sources reviewed here; no republic statute or local court decision is cited.

Enforcement data specific to Kabardino-Balkaria — propaganda cases, extremism charges, detentions or raids — is not sourced. The figures quoted (180 cases in 2023, 101 convictions to 30 June 2025, 60 million rubles in fines) are national.

The period covered by the UK Home Office note's systematic-campaign documentation runs to 2024; incidents after that date in this republic are not sourced, and Isteev's assessment of annual deterioration is not tied to specific dated events in Kabardino-Balkaria.

No source reviewed documents access to gender-affirming care, clinics, or support organisations operating openly within the republic, and none identifies current local services for trans visitors.

Whether US Level 4 and UK country policy guidance on Russia has been updated after mid-2025 is unresolved in this record.
